# Timeline

Answer field: `model` = `timeline:<topic id>`. Example: "Zeig mir den Zeitstrahl der Weltkriege" gives `timeline:world_wars`.

## Requirements

**Topics.** A closed list of 26 ids in `timeline_topics.h`, generated with the data. The prompt rule and `fetch()` both read that list, so they can't differ. An id not on the list returns false before any URL is built, and Zitro shows the normal Wikipedia picture.

**Data.** Prepared files on the Zitro server, generated by `scripts/make_timeline_data.py` into `webpage2/data/timeline/`:

- `<id>.txt`: UTF-8, tab-separated. Header: `ZTL1`, id, subject QID, title DE, title EN, event count, bundle bytes. One line per event: QID, year, end year or `-`, flags (1 circa, 2 the year is a birth, 4 the date is from Wikipedia), label DE, label EN, image offset, length, width, height, FNV-1a hash, credit or `-`.
- `<id>.jpgs`: all pictures of the timeline, baseline JPEG, one after the other.
- `credits.html`: maker, licence and file link of every picture.

**Dates.** Every date comes from Wikidata, except a few in `life_history` that come from Wikipedia (below). Wikidata is read in this order: P580, P585, P571, P575, P619, P606, P1619, P729, P577 (or the one property named for that event, such as P569 for a person's birth). Deprecated and no-value statements don't count, and preferred rank wins. These get an event rejected:
- no date
- precision coarser than a year (a million years for `dinosaurs` and `earth_history`, a hundred million years for `life_history`)
- several values with different years
- a year that differs from the person's expectation in the allow-list, which is only a cross-check. It caught the Colosseum (Wikidata 82, usually given as 80), which was then left out

Wikidata's "circa" qualifier (P1480) is shown as "ca.", a birth year (P569) as "geb." / "born". BC years are negative in Wikidata's JSON; checked with the assassination of Caesar, `-0044`.

**Dates from Wikipedia, only where Wikidata has none.** Approved by the user on 2026-11-09, used only by `life_history` so far. The allow-list names the article's language, title and revision ID, the sentence, and the year. The generator downloads exactly that revision and refuses the event unless the sentence stands in it and states the year's number ("3.5 billion years ago", "3,45 Milliarden Jahre alt"). A date from Wikipedia is always shown with "ca.". Each written number is read one way only, so a sentence whose number is ambiguous is refused, never misread. If Wikidata gains a usable date for the item later, the generator refuses the Wikipedia date and says so, and the allow-list entry has to change. Such an event carries flag 4 in the file, and the bottom line then names Wikipedia instead of Wikidata.

**Rough dates get "ca."** In `life_history` (`coarse_circa`), a date Wikidata knows less exactly than the stick writes it is shown with "ca.": coarser than a million years in deep time, coarser than a year after that. *Homo sapiens* (Wikidata: 200,000 years ago, to the nearest 100,000) shows as "ca. 200000 v. Chr.".

**Labels.** Wikidata labels in DE and EN, or `mul`. A label over 38 characters gives way to Wikidata's short name (P1813) or alias, the shortest of at least 8 characters, because shorter ones are bare abbreviations (WW2, HST). Missing DE or EN falls back to the other language and is logged. Labels with characters outside U+0020-U+05FF are refused. The tests wrap every label with the widths of the stick's real font and fail on any that would be cut.

**Pictures and child safety.** The audience starts at early readers and the topics include war, so no corpses, wounded people, atrocities or gore. For human evolution: reconstructions, skulls, skeletons and fossils are fine, nudity is not. How that is enforced:
1. `scripts/make_timeline_allowlist.py` names one exact Commons file per event, chosen by hand. Wikidata's own image is never used automatically: for Pearl Harbor it is an exploding ship, for Caesar's assassination a painting of the killing.
2. Topics marked `sensitive` (world wars, Cold War, Roman Empire, ancient Greece, Middle Ages, Swiss history) accept only the tags portrait, map, vehicle, flag, building, document, nature, artifact.
3. Commons categories are checked against a list of words (corpses, wounded, massacre, execution and so on). This is a second net, not the real check.
4. Every picture was looked at on captioned contact sheets at its prepared size, on 2026-11-06, and those of `life_history` on 2026-11-12. **The one who looked was the AI that built this, not a person.** A few were enlarged for a closer look; the rest were seen only at that small size, so a small detail could be missed.
5. A file Commons marks `trademarked` or `insignia` is refused, even with a free licence. This removed the 1924 Olympics poster; the Olympic rings had already been swapped for a stadium. No chosen file is marked `personality`.
6. `scripts/make_timeline_pins.py` pins each looked-at file by SHA-1. A changed Commons file is refused until someone looks again.

What the looking changed: "1944 NormandyLST.jpg" turned out to be soldiers wading ashore from a landing craft, despite its name, and was replaced by a plan drawing of the landing craft. A photo of a young child getting polio drops was removed. A nuclear missile on parade, Wikidata's image for the Cuban Missile Crisis, was replaced by a map.

For `life_history`, three pictures were turned down while choosing, before the sheet: Wikidata's image for *Homo sapiens* ("Human.svg", a nude couple, which the category check also refuses), a full-body "Lucy" reconstruction with bare breasts, and an Archaeopteryx painting in which it pounces on a small dinosaur. Lucy is now a head-and-shoulders reconstruction, Archaeopteryx the Berlin fossil, and the three *Homo* species are skulls. Nothing on the finished sheet had to be replaced. The picture for insects (about 400 million years ago) is a model of Meganeura, a giant dragonfly from about 300 million years ago.

**Decision for a person:** nobody has looked at these pictures except the AI. `make_timeline_data.py --contact-sheets <dir>` writes the sheets, one per topic, so they can be skimmed in a few minutes.

**Deliberately left out.** The world wars timeline doesn't name the Holocaust or the atomic bombings, and shows no Nazi symbols and no portraits of perpetrators. Pearl Harbor shows the memorial, Sarajevo a portrait of the Archduke. The picture for Pearl Harbor is the memorial, with the sunken ship visible under the water. The Black Death has no picture. This is a choice about what suits the youngest users, not a statement about history, and it needs a person's decision.

`life_history` leaves out the eukaryotes (cells with a nucleus), although the spec named them. Wikidata dates them to 2.7 billion years ago, and English Wikipedia (revision 1385070551) says the biomarkers behind that date "have been rebutted as later contaminants". Wikidata has a date, so the rules don't allow taking Wikipedia's instead.

**Fetch.** `<id>.txt` must arrive, within 12 s, or there is no timeline. Then `<id>.jpgs` into PSRAM as a single download, because every extra file would cost another TLS handshake. Total limit 30 s instead of `EDU_LOOKUP_DEADLINE_MS`. Limits: 24 events, 8 KB index, 512 KB bundle. Today's largest bundle is 112 KB (`life_history`, 20 pictures).

**A picture is kept only if** all of it arrived, it starts and ends as a JPEG, and its hash matches the index. Otherwise that event has no picture, and the timeline still works. After a stalled download, the pictures that arrived whole are kept. No PSRAM for the bundle: a timeline without pictures.

**Screen.**
- Top line: the time axis. Year marks at one spacing per timeline, gold dots for events.
- Band: picture 240x96 at most. Contained for maps, flags, portraits, documents and artworks, otherwise cropped to fill.
- Year: big, top left, fixed in place, running across a gap. BC as "v. Chr." / "BC", from a million years as "Mio. Jahre her" / "million years ago", from a billion years as "Mrd. Jahre her" / "billion years ago" ("3,45" / "3.45"). An end year if Wikidata has one; in deep time only if it is a million years or more back, so *Homo erectus* shows "1,9" without its end 143,000 years ago.
- Label: up to two lines, broken at spaces and hyphens, under the picture.
- Bottom line: the picture's credit where its licence asks for one, otherwise the timeline's name and "Wikidata", or "Wikipedia" for a date taken from there (flag 4). A credit wider than the line shows its licence alone, the text after the last ", ", as on the dinosaur sheet (`dinoCreditLicence`). It is measured in the font the line uses: DejaVu9, or the 12 pt font for a credit with letters outside ASCII. Right side: `3/8`, or "Ende"/"End" on the last event.

**Spacing.** Each picture fills the screen and takes no time: its year stays while it's on screen. Only the empty gap between two pictures means time. One scale per timeline, set so the median gap is 120 px, so equal time is an equal gap. Limits: 24 px minimum, 720 px maximum. A time cut to the maximum is marked by a break in the axis, and it can't be read as to scale. Year marks and the running year use the gap only. A gap of at least 110 px has the time written in it ("21 Jahre").

**Input.**
- Button C: next event. On the last event it goes to the text answer, and the next visit starts at the first event. That is the way out; Button A (new question) also works everywhere.
- Button B: previous event. Stops at the first.
- Tilt: tipping the stick about 20 degrees around the axis through its screen, right side down, moves one event forward; left side down moves back. Going back to level does nothing. Tilt stops at both ends and never leaves the view. Uses `modelGyroDps[2]`, dead zone 15 degrees per second. The direction is the constant `TIMELINE_TILT_SIGN`.

**Performance.** One picture decoded per frame at most, into one of 5 PSRAM sprites (46 KB each) kept for the current event and its neighbours. Pictures are never decoded per frame once in a sprite. Every 5 s the serial log prints `Timeline frame: draw avg .. max .. ms, period avg .. ms, N decodes avg .. max .. ms, ...`. Expect one decode to be visible as a short hitch at the start of a move; this is unmeasured on the stick.

**Not tested on the stick:** everything on the device, including the tilt direction, frame time, decode time, the fetch against the live server, and how `life_history` looks ("Mrd. Jahre her", 20 events). Its files are on zitro.spot (checked over HTTPS on 2026-11-14). `model timeline:world_wars` on the serial port tries it.

**Tests.** `tests/timeline/run.sh`: parser with broken and hostile input, picture checks, layout, motion, tilt gesture, year text, label wrap, and every generated file. It also decodes all pictures with `lgfx_tjpgd`, the decoder behind `drawJpg`. Measured here: 183 pictures, average 4.9 KB, largest 11 KB, all decoded without error. Decode time on this computer says nothing about the stick.

## User guide

Ask for a timeline: "Zeig mir den Zeitstrahl der Weltkriege" or "Show me a timeline of space exploration". "Zeig mir den Zeitstrahl der Geschichte des Lebens" or "Show me a timeline of the history of life" goes from the first cells, about 3.5 billion years ago, to us.

Topics: world wars, space exploration, dinosaurs, Roman Empire, inventions, Swiss history, ancient Egypt, ancient Greece, Middle Ages, explorers, aviation, railways, computers, Moon missions, Mars missions, Olympic Games, medicine, scientists, composers, painters, Earth's history, Cold War, famous buildings, communication, cars, the history of life.

- **Button C:** next event. After the last one you're back at the answer.
- **Button B:** previous event.
- **Tip the stick** to the right for the next event, to the left for the previous one.
- **Button A:** new question.

The big year runs while the band moves. A long empty stretch between two pictures means a long time. A small cut in the line at the top means even longer than it looks.

## Release note

- Ask for a timeline and travel through history: tip Zitro or press a button to go from the first satellite to the Moon, with real dates and pictures.
- From the first cells to you: ask "Zeig mir den Zeitstrahl der Geschichte des Lebens" and travel 3.5 billion years, past the first fish, the dinosaurs and Lucy, all the way to us.

## Sources and licences

- **Wikidata:** dates and labels. CC0, no credit required.
- **Wikipedia:** 7 dates in `life_history`, each a number from one sentence of a named revision (de or en). Only the number is used. Where the bottom line shows no picture credit (the licence needs none, or the picture didn't arrive), it says "Wikipedia" for these events and "Wikidata" for the others. After the timeline, the answer's bottom line still says "Wikidata" for the timeline as a whole, which is where its labels and most dates come from.
- **Wikimedia Commons:** pictures. Licences used: public domain 84, CC0 7, CC BY 27, CC BY-SA 65. Checked per file from Commons metadata. NC, ND, fair use and GFDL alone are refused. CC BY and CC BY-SA need the maker's name: shown on the bottom line where it fits, and always in `credits.html` with the licence, a link to the file and a note that it was resized and may be cropped. Where Commons' metadata names nobody, the name is copied from the file page into the allow-list (4 files).
- **CC BY-SA means** the resized pictures stay under the same licence.
- Not fully tidy: `credits.html` shows the author text as Commons gives it, such as "The original uploader was HPH at German Wikipedia", but without e-mail addresses, which a public page must not republish. The bottom line falls back to the licence alone where maker and licence don't fit: the generator writes the licence alone above 60 bytes, and the stick shows the licence alone when the credit is wider than the line.
- `credits.html` must be uploaded with the data, at `https://zitro.spot/data/timeline/credits.html`. The website links it in its Sources list (item 9 of `webpage2/index.html`). Whether a credit file counts as "available" enough is a decision for a person.
